newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Last Russian combat unit to leave Chechnya Sunday.
newsitem.headline: Last Russian combat unit to leave Chechnya Sunday.

text.p: Russia on Sunday prepared to pull out its last combat unit from Chechnya under a peace deal between Moscow and separatist leaders paving way for crucial regional elections next month.

Itar-Tass news agency quoted Russian military command in Chechnya as saying that units of the 205th Motor Rifle brigade were expected to board planes on Sunday and leave from Khankala airbase outside the regional capital Grozny.
The military told Tass only logistics and transport units would remain in Chechnya pending a final pullout next month.

"Now the coalition government will carry full responsibility for the situation in the region," Tass quoted Ivan Rybkin, secretary of President Boris Yeltsin's policy-making Security Council, as saying in refrence to the separatist leadership.
Under the peace deal signed on August 31 Moscow promised to withdraw its forces, which were sent to Chechnya in December 1994 to quell the southern region's independence bid.
Tens of thousands of people have died in 21 months of the ill-fated war in which Russian troops have suffered many humiliating defeats .
The rebels, for their part, agreed to postpone by five years the decision on Chechnya's political status. But their leaders make little secret that they still want full independence.

Under their pressure President Boris Yeltsin earlier this month abandoned the idea of keeping the 205th brigade and another brigade of Interior Ministry forces permanently in Chechnya and ordered a complete withdrawal.
The separatist leadership has called local elections for January 27 to elect a Chechen president and parliament. They are pressing Moscow to complete the pullout by the day of the polls.

Moscow officials have said that unless any unexpected complications arise the withdrawal will be completed several days before the polls in which all major Chechen resistance leaders will run for president.

Five candidates -- separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, premier Aslan Maskhadov, prominent field commander Shamil Basayev, security supremo Akhmed Zakayev and propaganda chief Movladi Udugov, have so far provided the electoral commission with 10,000 signatures of support.
The five known as "resistance candidates" have failed in their attempts to rally behind a single candidate but have vowed to stick together after the polls.

The runup to the election was soured earlier this month by the killing by unidentified gunmen of six foreign aid workers who had been running a hospital in central Chechnya. Several ethnic Russian families have also been killed in a string of attacks in Grozny.

Foreign aid agencies have decied to freeze their operations in Chechnya for security reasons and U.N. officials have said that fear of violence could hamper plans by foreign observers to monitor the polls.

Both Russians and rebels agree that unidentified forces keen to derail the fragile peace process were behind the attacks. But each side has tried to use the killings, none of which has been solved so far, for its own political interests.

Russian officials have accused the rebels of being unable to maintain order in the province. Separatist leaders have hinted that rogue elements of the Russian security forces may have been behind the attacks.
